title: Homeland Security and Further Additional Continuing Appropriations Act, 2026
official_title: Making further consolidated appropriations for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2026, and for other purposes.
summary: After a 75-day partial DHS shutdown triggered by lapsed appropriations, this bill provided the Department of Homeland Security with its full-year FY2026 budget — the first dedicated annual appropriations act for DHS in this cycle. Division A is the complete DHS Appropriations Act, funding all major department components through September 30, 2026. Division B extends the existing governmentwide continuing resolution (Public Law 119-37) for other unfunded federal agencies and retroactively covers the appropriations lapse that began on or about February 14, 2026. The law also authorizes back pay for furloughed federal employees and retroactively ratifies obligations made during the shutdown to maintain essential operations.
brief: Ended a 75-day partial DHS shutdown with the department's first full-year FY2026 appropriations — $11.08B for CBP, $10.64B for TSA, $11.27B for the Coast Guard, and $26.4B in the FEMA disaster relief fund — plus a short-term CR for remaining unfunded agencies through May 22.

top_lines.headline: DHS Shutdown Ends — Back Pay Authorized
subs: The partial DHS shutdown, which began February 14, 2026, is ended — 75 days after the previous continuing resolution expired
Furloughed federal employees are authorized to receive back pay; obligations incurred during the shutdown are retroactively ratified

top_lines.headline: Border and Enforcement Agencies Fully Funded
subs: CBP receives $11.08B for operations and support plus $222.9M for construction and improvements
TSA receives $10.64B for operations; Coast Guard receives $11.27B including $530M for defense-related activities
Secret Service receives $3.13B with up to $40M for premium pay above standard caps

top_lines.headline: FEMA Disaster Relief Fund — $26.37B
subs: $26.4B appropriated to the FEMA Disaster Relief Fund for major disaster declarations
$494M for State Homeland Security grants; $300M for Nonprofit Security grants split between high-risk urban and non-urban areas
$684M for firefighter grants under the SAFER and Assistance to Firefighter programs

top_lines.headline: Coast Guard MQ-9 Drone Program
subs: $98M for Coast Guard procurement of MQ-9 unmanned aircraft and base stations
Explicitly prohibits equipping any long-range unmanned aircraft with kinetic capabilities — no weapons on government drones

likelihoodReason: Signed into law by the President on April 30, 2026 as Public Law 119-86.

sections.label: Title II — Security, Enforcement, and Investigations

items.main: Provides full-year FY2026 appropriations for CBP, TSA, Coast Guard, and Secret Service through September 30, 2026.
items.detail: CBP operations and support: $11.08B (includes unaccompanied minor transportation, air/marine law enforcement support, and up to 7,500 police vehicles). CBP construction: $222.9M with border security infrastructure funded through September 2030. TSA operations: $10.64B (offsetting aviation security fee collections reduce the general fund share to approximately $7.61B). Coast Guard operations: $11.27B including $530M for defense-related activities and $24.5M from the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund. Coast Guard construction: $991.9M available through September 2030. USSS operations: $3.13B with up to $40M in premium pay above standard limits and a $2M grant for Missing and Exploited Children investigations.

sections.label: Title III — Protection, Preparedness, Response, and Recovery

items.main: Funds CISA and FEMA including a $26.37B Disaster Relief Fund appropriation and $3.84B in Federal Assistance grants.
items.detail: CISA operations and support: $2.22B plus $386.5M for construction. FEMA operations: $1.67B. FEMA federal assistance grants: $3.84B, allocated across State Homeland Security ($494M), Urban Area Security Initiative ($584M), Nonprofit Security ($300M, split evenly between high-risk urban and non-urban areas), firefighter grants ($684M across SAFER and AFG), Port Security ($95M), emergency management performance ($337M), and flood hazard mapping ($297M). Disaster Relief Fund: $26.4B for major disaster declarations under the Stafford Act.

items.main: Includes $20M for body-worn cameras for ICE and CBP agents, $98M for Coast Guard MQ-9 drones, and bans new land border crossing fees.
items.detail: Sec. 109 appropriates $20M for body-worn cameras for agents performing immigration enforcement, with a 30-day spend plan requirement. Sec. 204 prohibits the Secretary from establishing, collecting, or studying any new border crossing fee at land ports of entry on the Southern or Northern border. Sec. 207 limits border surveillance procurement to autonomous systems as defined in Pub. L. 119-21. Sec. 208 requires CBP to maintain its November 2021 policy protecting pregnant women in custody. Sec. 219 provides $98M for Coast Guard MQ-9 aircraft and prohibits equipping any long-range unmanned aircraft with kinetic capabilities. Sec. 222 restricts Secret Service protection of federal agency heads to DHS Secretary only; all other agency-head protection must be on a reimbursable basis.

sections.label: Division B — Further Additional Continuing Appropriations

items.main: Extends FY2025 appropriations rates for agencies not covered by a full-year bill through the earlier of May 22, 2026, or enactment of applicable full-year appropriations.
items.detail: Retroactively ratifies obligations incurred during the partial DHS shutdown that were necessary to maintain essential operations to protect life and property. Authorizes back pay, in accordance with current law, for federal employees who were furloughed or required to work without pay during the partial shutdown.

underreported.section: Section 209 — No TSA Exemptions for Officials
underreported.summary: Members of Congress, Cabinet secretaries, agency heads, and senior White House staff are explicitly barred from exemptions from federal passenger and baggage screening. A separate provision bars future legislation from overriding this requirement using funds from this act.
underreported.why_unreported: Appropriations bills frequently include policy riders that never surface in coverage of the headline funding numbers. This provision directly names elected officials and executive appointees as subject to the same screening requirements as the public.

underreported.section: Section 227 — Canadian Prescription Drug Imports Protected
underreported.summary: CBP is barred from preventing individuals from importing up to a 90-day personal-use supply of prescription drugs from Canada that comply with FDA standards. Controlled substances and biological products are excluded.
underreported.why_unreported: This carve-out for Canadian drug imports sits quietly inside a DHS spending bill and has significant implications for border enforcement priorities around pharmaceutical imports.

underreported.section: Section 204 — No New Border Crossing Fees
underreported.summary: The Secretary of Homeland Security is prohibited from establishing, collecting, or studying any new fee charged to pedestrians, cyclists, or vehicle occupants crossing the Southern or Northern border at a land port of entry.
underreported.why_unreported: Border crossing fees have been discussed as a potential revenue mechanism. This provision explicitly blocks even a feasibility study, making it a quiet but firm policy prohibition embedded in the appropriations text.

criticisms.why: this morning, Democrats sent Republicans our counteroffer on legislation to reopen DHS, pay TSA workers, while at the same time rein in ICE with commonsense guardrails. Our offer is a reasonable, good-faith proposal that contains some of the very same asks Democrats have been talking about now for months.

The funding year ends at the end of September, so we are talking about something closer to 26 weeks. While there might be a cheer for 2 weeks, there would also be a lot of dread, and people across the Nation would be going: So the proposal is to fund for 2 weeks while the majority sends us out for a 2-week break.

There is a provision in this, which I am not sure that you are aware of. It is very important. It is at the end of the second page, and it says about the effective date of this. This section shall apply on and after the day after the date of the regularly scheduled general election for Federal office held in November 2026. I don't want to wait until November, and I think that is an approach which puts that date in play.

gaps: Division B provides a short-term CR only through May 22, 2026 — remaining federal agencies without full-year appropriations will need further action before that date.

The Senate failed cloture 7 times between February 12 and March 26, 2026, repeatedly falling short of 60 votes. The bill ultimately passed without a recorded Senate floor vote, most likely via unanimous consent after a deal was struck.
No floor debate quotes are available — the bill appears to have cleared the Senate procedurally rather than through extended floor debate.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Thune
featured_quotes.text: we are on day 40 of Democrats' shutdown of Department of Homeland Security--day 40. And that is on top of Democrats' recordbreaking 43-day full-government shutdown in the fall. Altogether, thanks to Senate Democrats, a lot of DHS employees have been working without pay for more than 80 days so far this fiscal year. That is shameful. It is no wonder TSA agents are quitting in droves-- anyone would be if they had been working without pay for almost 50 percent of the fiscal year so far.
